fetched_contents.title: Aphasia - NHS
fetched_contents.text: Aphasia Symptoms of aphasia Aphasia causes problems with communication including speaking, understanding others, reading and writing. It affects people in different ways, but symptoms may include: * not being able to say the right words , speaking very slowly or with long pauses * finding it very difficult to speak, or speaking in very short or incomplete sentences * repeating, mixing up or missing out words * making up words or sounds * not being able to understand what other people are saying, particularly if you cannot see them * difficulty reading or writing Causes of aphasia Aphasia is caused by damage to the parts of the brain that deal with language. Common causes include: * stroke – this is the most common cause of aphasia * severe head injury * a brain tumour, or bleeding or an infection in the brain * conditions that cause the brain to become damaged over time, like dementia, or alcohol or drug-related brain damage Anyone can get aphasia, but it's more common in people over 65. This is because the risk of stroke and conditions like dementia is higher for older people. There are different types of aphasia depending on which part of your brain has been affected. Immediate action required: Call 999 if: You or someone you're with suddenly has: * face weakness – one side of your face may droop (fall) and it might be hard to smile * weakness or numbness in one arm or down one side of your body – you may not be able to fully lift both arms and keep them there * speech problems – you may slur your words, sound confused, or find it difficult to speak or find the right words * blurred vision or loss of sight in one or both eyes These can be signs of a stroke, which needs to be treated immediately. Information: Do not drive yourself to A&E. The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do. Treatment for aphasia Aphasia is treated with speech and language therapy. A speech and language therapist can assess your symptoms and work with you to improve your speaking, reading and writing. They can help you to find different ways to communicate. Treatment depends on your symptoms but can include: * matching words to pictures * categorising or sorting words * repeating words or rhyming tasks * practising ways of communicating without words, like drawing, body language, hand movements and facial expressions * using technology – for example, setting your phone to be voice-activated or taking pictures of things you struggle to name * recommending speech and language therapy apps or computer programs to help you practise Speech and language therapy may be done individually, in a group, face to face or online. It also usually involves the people around you, like your family or friends, and anyone who may help care for you. Living with aphasia There is currently no cure for aphasia. How much it affects your life varies from person to person, and depends on the cause and amount of damage to the brain. It can be very frustrating, confusing and difficult if you or someone you know has aphasia. It can affect people's relationships and independence in daily life, and cause anxiety, low mood and depression, loneliness or isolation. Talking therapies and support from your care team can help with these problems. If aphasia was caused by a stroke, head injury or brain tumour, most people improve with treatment, especially in the first few months. People can still improve months or years later, and some do recover fully. If aphasia is caused by a condition that gets worse over time, like dementia, the symptoms are likely to get worse. Treatment may focus on learning and practising other ways of communicating, like drawing, body language or using technology. Speech and language therapy should help, and there are things you and others can do to help manage aphasia. Help and support for aphasia Aphasia can be a difficult condition to live with, practically and emotionally. As well as support from your doctor and speech and language therapist, you may find it helpful to get support from other people with aphasia, either at a local group or online. There are also national charities that can offer support and information about aphasia. fetched_contents.title: Dysarthria (difficulty speaking) - NHS
fetched_contents.text: Dysarthria (difficulty speaking) Dysarthria is where you have difficulty speaking because the muscles you use for speech are weak. It can be caused by conditions that damage your brain or nerves and some medicines. Speech and language therapy can help. Immediate action required: Call 999 if: * somebody's face droops on 1 side (the mouth or eye may have drooped) * a person cannot lift up both arms and keep them there * a person has difficulty speaking (speech may be slurred or garbled) These can be signs of a stroke, which is a medical emergency. The symptoms of a stroke usually come on suddenly. Information: Do not drive yourself to A&E. The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do. Symptoms of dysarthria The main symptom of dysarthria is unclear speech. This can make it difficult for you to make yourself understood. Your speech may only be slightly unclear, or you may not be able to speak clearly at all. Other symptoms include: * difficulty moving your mouth, tongue or lips * slurred or slow speech * difficulty controlling the volume of your voice, making you talk too loudly or quietly * a change in your voice, making it nasal, strained or monotone * hesitating a lot when talking, or speaking in short bursts instead of full sentences Being stressed or tired may make your symptoms worse. Information: Dysarthria is not the same as dysphasia, although you can have both conditions at the same time. Dysphasia, also known as aphasia, is where you have difficulty understanding words or putting them together in a sentence. Non-urgent advice: See a GP if: * you've noticed gradual changes to your or your child's speech and you're worried They'll examine you and may refer you to a specialist for further tests. Causes of dysarthria Dysarthria is usually caused by damage to the brain or conditions that affect the nervous system. It can happen at any age. Common causes include: * stroke, severe head injury and brain tumours * Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis and motor neurone disease * cerebral palsy and Down's syndrome It can also be a side effect of certain medicines, such as some medicines to treat epilepsy. Treatment for dysarthria If you have dysarthria, you'll usually be referred to a speech and language therapist. They'll offer therapy to help your speech and communication. The therapy you're offered will be different depending on the cause of your dysarthria and how severe it is. Some people may find therapy does not help their symptoms, or their speech may get worse as their condition progresses. Their therapy may focus on helping communication in other ways. Branch report on reassurance and family communication

When explaining the situation to family, it’s important to be clear but reassuring: the main idea is that sudden jumbled speech or word-finding difficulty can be serious, but it can also sometimes be less urgent. You can say something like, “Grandma is having trouble speaking or finding words, which worries us because it could be something like a stroke, but it might also be another condition that needs medical attention.” Then add, “The important thing is to see a doctor quickly so they can check what’s going on and decide whether it’s something urgent or something that can wait.” That keeps family members informed without causing unnecessary alarm [N1-R1][N5-F3][N7-R2].

What to share with the doctor is straightforward: write down what you’ve noticed, when it started, whether it came on suddenly or gradually, and whether anything makes it better or worse. Include any other symptoms, such as weakness, confusion, drooping face, trouble seeing, or dizziness, because those are red flags for stroke or other serious conditions [N2-F2][N5-F3]. You should also note if Grandma has a history of stroke, dementia, thyroid problems, or sleep issues, because those can change the likely diagnosis [N3-R2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

Interpreting the doctor’s explanation in plain language depends on what they say. If they say it’s “aphasia,” that means difficulty with language, especially speaking and understanding words [N1-R1][N1-R2]. If they say it’s “dysarthria,” it means the muscles used for speech are weak, so speech sounds slurred or unclear [N5-R1][N5-F3]. If they say it’s a stroke, that means the brain’s blood supply was interrupted suddenly, and it needs fast treatment [N2-F2][N7-R5]. If they think it’s related to dementia or age-related change, they’ll usually explain that speech problems can be a sign of early dementia or slow brain changes, but that doesn’t mean Grandma is “getting worse” right away [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The key is to ask the doctor to repeat any medical terms and use simple words so everyone understands.

Overall, the best reassurance is that doctors are trained to check for serious causes first, and that many speech problems have treatable or manageable causes. The main message for family is: “We should see a doctor soon, but we don’t know for sure yet—this is why we’re being careful” [N5-F3][N7-R2].

During a speech-related exam, the doctor will focus on two main areas: whether the problem is a language issue or a speech-muscle issue, and whether it started suddenly or slowly. The most relevant parts of the exam are the neurological exam and the assessment of speech itself [N6-R1][N6-F4]. The neurological exam checks mental status, motor function, balance, reflexes, and sensory function, because stroke and other brain problems often affect more than just speech [N6-F4]. The doctor will also look at facial movement, arm strength, and coordination, because stroke symptoms often include drooping on one side of the face, weakness in one arm, and slurred speech [N2-F2][N5-F3].

The tests most commonly used to confirm a cause depend on the suspected diagnosis. For sudden speech problems, the doctor may start with a neurological exam and ask the patient to repeat words, follow directions, or speak aloud [N6-R1][N6-F4]. If a serious condition is suspected, they may order brain imaging such as a CT scan or MRI to look for stroke, brain tumors, or other structural problems [N1-R4][N3-R3]. They may also do blood tests to check for thyroid problems, infection, or other treatable causes [N4-R1][N4-R5]. If dementia is being considered, the doctor may ask about memory, behavior, and other cognitive symptoms, because dementia-related speech changes often come gradually and are linked to memory and language problems [N3-R2][N3-R3].

Early versus late findings change the diagnosis in a key way. If the problem started suddenly and is accompanied by face drooping, arm weakness, or confusion, the doctor will treat it as a possible stroke or acute brain injury and act quickly [N2-F2][N7-R2]. If the problem is gradual and is linked to older age, memory changes, or a slowly progressive condition, the doctor is more likely to consider dementia, brain degeneration, or a slowly growing tumor [N1-R4][N3-R2][N3-R3]. The earlier the symptoms appear and the more sudden they are, the more urgent the investigation becomes [N1-R4][N7-R2].

In plain language, the doctor is likely to say something like: “I’ll check your speech, movement, and reflexes to see where the problem is coming from,” or “We need to rule out stroke right away because those symptoms can be serious.” If they’re unsure, they’ll probably schedule imaging or specialist tests and talk about whether Grandma should see a neurologist, speech therapist, or other specialist [N6-R3][N6-F4][N7-R3].

## Integrated answer for you and your family

Your question is a common one: “Grandma’s speech messed up, words are jumbled, not sure if normal or serious or if I gotta do anything.” The short answer is: **this can be serious, and it is definitely worth doing something right away, but the exact answer depends on what is happening and how quickly it started.** Below is a practical breakdown of what you should know, what to do next, and how to explain it to your family.

---

## 1) Most likely causes: aphasia, dysarthria, stroke, dementia, or something else

The branch reports point to a few main possibilities:

### **A. Aphasia**
Aphasia is a language disorder that makes it hard to speak, understand others, read, or write [N1-R1][N1-R2]. It often happens suddenly after a stroke or head injury, but it can also come on gradually from a slow-growing brain tumor or brain damage from conditions like dementia [N1-R4][N1-F1]. The NHS says aphasia is the most common cause of sudden speech problems [N1-F1]. So if Grandma suddenly has trouble finding words or slurred speech, aphasia is a strong possibility [N1-R1][N1-R4].

### **B. Dysarthria**
Dysarthria is a speech-muscle problem that causes slurred or unclear speech because the muscles used for speech are weak [N5-R1][N5-F3]. It can be caused by stroke, head injury, brain tumors, or medicines [N5-F3][N7-R4]. If Grandma’s speech sounds mumbled or hard to understand but she can still form words, dysarthria may be the cause [N5-R1][N5-F3].

### **C. Stroke**
Stroke is especially worrisome because sudden speech problems are one of its classic red flags. The NHS says to call 999 if someone suddenly has face weakness, arm weakness, or speech problems [N2-F2][N5-F3]. If Grandma’s jumbled speech is sudden and is accompanied by one-sided weakness, confusion, or slurred speech, stroke is the most urgent concern [N2-F2][N7-R5].

### **D. Dementia or cognitive decline**
Dementia-related language loss can also cause word-finding difficulty and speech changes. Dementia can damage the brain parts that control language, and subtle speech changes are sometimes linked to early Alzheimer’s-related brain changes [N3-R2][N3-R3]. But the branch reports also note that these usually develop gradually and are not the same as sudden speech block [N3-R2][N3-R3]. If Grandma’s symptoms are slow and only mildly affect speech, dementia may be one possibility, but it is still important to check.

### **E. Other non-stroke causes**
Other possible causes include thyroid problems, sleep apnea, and medication side effects [N4-R1][N4-R5]. These are less urgent than stroke, but still worth ruling out because they can affect speech and communication [N4-R1][N4-R5].

So, the most likely diagnosis is not a single fixed answer. The branch reports suggest that **aphasia, stroke, dysarthria, dementia, and other medical causes** are the main possibilities, depending on how the symptoms started and what else is happening [N1-R1][N1-R4][N5-R1][N2-F2][N3-R2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

---

## 2) Which symptoms suggest a serious or urgent problem?

The branch reports make this very clear: **sudden speech changes with sudden weakness, confusion, or facial drooping are red flags for stroke or acute brain injury** [N2-F2][N5-F3][N7-R5].

### **Red flags for urgent care**
- **Sudden slurred speech or confusion** [N2-F2][N5-F3]
- **Face weakness or drooping** [N2-F2][N5-F3]
- **Weakness in one arm or down one side of the body** [N2-F2][N5-F3]
- **Difficulty finding words** [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Sudden trouble reading or writing** [N1-R1][N1-F1]

The NHS says stroke symptoms often come on suddenly, so anything that happens abruptly and is not explained by tiredness or a minor cold should be treated as urgent [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### **What does not mean it’s urgent**
If Grandma’s speech changes are **gradual**, **mild**, and **not accompanied by sudden weakness, confusion, or facial drooping**, it is less likely to be an emergency. The branch reports say that normal age-related changes can include slower speech or mild word-finding difficulty, but they are usually mild and do not come on suddenly [N3-R2][N3-R3]. However, even slow changes should be checked by a doctor, especially in older adults, because stroke and dementia-related changes are more common [N1-R4][N3-R2].

---

## 3) How to differentiate normal age-related changes from something concerning

The branch reports say the key is **gradualness** and **whether other symptoms are present** [N3-R2][N3-R3].

### **Normal age-related changes**
- Gradual slowing of speech or mild difficulty finding words [N3-R2][N3-R3]
- Mild forgetfulness or mild confusion that comes and goes [N3-R2]
- Speech changes that are mild and not suddenly severe [N3-R2]

### **Something concerning**
- Sudden speech changes [N1-R4][N2-F2][N7-R2]
- Sudden weakness, confusion, or facial drooping [N2-F2][N5-F3]
- Sudden trouble reading, writing, or understanding others [N1-R1][N1-F1]

In plain language: if Grandma’s speech problem is slow and only slightly changes her ability to speak, it may still need a doctor’s check, but it is less likely to be an emergency. If it started suddenly and is joined by other serious symptoms, it is very likely serious and needs fast action [N3-R2][N3-R3][N2-F2].

---

## 4) What to do next: next steps and when to act

The branch reports say the next steps depend on **when the problem started**, **how sudden it was**, and **whether other symptoms are present** [N5-F3][N7-R1][N6-F4].

### **What to observe or record before seeing a doctor**
Write down:
- When the problem started
- Whether it came on suddenly or gradually
- What Grandma is saying or struggling to say
- Any other symptoms, such as weakness, drooping face, dizziness, confusion, or trouble seeing [N2-F2][N5-F3]
- Whether Grandma is more confused, slower, or more tired
- Whether anything makes the speech problem better or worse [N5-F3]

Keeping this note helps the doctor decide how urgently to act [N5-F3].

### **When to seek emergency care**
If Grandma’s speech changes are **sudden** and are accompanied by:
- Face weakness or drooping
- Arm weakness
- Slurred speech
- Confusion
- Sudden difficulty reading or writing
you should **call emergency services right away** [N2-F2][N5-F3][N7-R2]. The NHS specifically says to call 999 if someone suddenly has face weakness, arm weakness, or speech problems [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### **When to schedule an appointment**
If the problem is **gradual** and not accompanied by sudden weakness, confusion, or other serious symptoms, a GP appointment is usually the next step [N5-F3][N7-R1]. However, even slow speech changes should not be ignored because they can still be linked to stroke, dementia, or other treatable causes [N1-R4][N3-R2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

### **What kind of specialist or tests are usually needed**
A doctor is likely to:
- Do a **neurological exam** to check mental status, motor function, balance, reflexes, and sensory function [N6-F4]
- Order **brain imaging** such as a CT scan or MRI to look for stroke, brain tumors, or other structural problems [N1-R4][N6-F4]
- Do **blood tests** to check for thyroid problems, infection, or other treatable causes [N4-R1][N4-R5]
- Ask about **memory, behavior, and other cognitive symptoms** if dementia is suspected [N3-R2][N3-R3]
- Refer to a **neurologist, speech and language therapist, or other specialist** if the cause is not clear [N6-R3][N6-F4]

So, the likely next steps are:
1. **Call emergency services if sudden and serious symptoms are present** [N2-F2][N5-F3]
2. **Record details of what happened** [N5-F3]
3. **See the doctor soon** [N5-F3][N7-R1]
4. **Expect a neurological exam and tests** [N6-F4][N6-R3]

---

## 5) How to explain this to family in a reassuring way

The branch reports suggest a clear but reassuring way to explain it to family:

- **Be direct but calm:** “Grandma is having trouble speaking or finding words, which worries us because it could be something like a stroke, but it might also be another condition that needs medical attention.” [N1-R1][N5-F3][N7-R2]
- **Explain why it matters:** “The important thing is to see a doctor soon so they can check what’s going on and decide whether it’s something urgent or something that can wait.” [N5-F3][N7-R2]
- **Be honest about uncertainty:** “We don’t know for sure yet, but this is why we’re being careful.” [N5-F3][N7-R2]

What to share with the doctor:
- What Grandma is saying or struggling to say
- When the problem started
- Whether it came on suddenly or gradually
- Any other symptoms, such as weakness, drooping face, dizziness, confusion, or trouble seeing [N2-F2][N5-F3]
- Any history of stroke, dementia, thyroid problems, or sleep issues [N3-R2][N4-R1][N4-R5]

How to interpret the doctor’s explanation:

### **B. Dysarthria**
Dysarthria is a speech-muscle problem that causes slurred or unclear speech because the muscles used for speech are weak [N5-R1][N5-F3]. It can be caused by stroke, head injury, brain tumors, or medicines [N5-F3][N7-R4]. If Grandma’s speech sounds mumbled or hard to understand but she can still form words, dysarthria may be the cause [N5-R1][N5-F3].

## Integrated answer for you and your family

Your question is a common one: “Grandma’s speech messed up, words are jumbled, not sure if normal or serious or if I gotta do anything.” The short answer is: **this can be serious, and it is definitely worth doing something right away, but the exact answer depends on what is happening and how quickly it started.** Below is a practical breakdown of what you should know, what to do next, and how to explain it to your family.

---

## 1) Most likely causes: aphasia, dysarthria, stroke, dementia, or something else

The branch reports point to a few main possibilities:

### **A. Aphasia**
Aphasia is a language disorder that makes it hard to speak, understand others, read, or write [N1-R1][N1-R2]. It often happens suddenly after a stroke or head injury, but it can also come on gradually from a slow-growing brain tumor or brain damage from conditions like dementia [N1-R4][N1-F1]. The NHS says aphasia is the most common cause of sudden speech problems [N1-F1]. So if Grandma suddenly has trouble finding words or slurred speech, aphasia is a strong possibility [N1-R1][N1-R4].

### **B. Dysarthria**
Dysarthria is a speech-muscle problem that causes slurred or unclear speech because the muscles used for speech are weak [N5-R1][N5-F3]. It can be caused by stroke, head injury, brain tumors, or medicines [N5-F3][N7-R4]. If Grandma’s speech sounds mumbled or hard to understand but she can still form words, dysarthria may be the cause [N5-R1][N5-F3].

### **C. Stroke**
Stroke is especially worrisome because sudden speech problems are one of its classic red flags. The NHS says to call 999 if someone suddenly has face weakness, arm weakness, or speech problems [N2-F2][N5-F3]. If Grandma’s jumbled speech is sudden and is accompanied by one-sided weakness, confusion, or slurred speech, stroke is the most urgent concern [N2-F2][N7-R5].

### **D. Dementia or cognitive decline**
Dementia-related language loss can also cause word-finding difficulty and speech changes. Dementia can damage the brain parts that control language, and subtle speech changes are sometimes linked to early Alzheimer’s-related brain changes [N3-R2][N3-R3]. But the branch reports also note that these usually develop gradually and are not the same as sudden speech block [N3-R2][N3-R3]. If Grandma’s symptoms are slow and only mildly affect speech, dementia may be one possibility, but it is still important to check.

### **E. Other non-stroke causes**
Other possible causes include thyroid problems, sleep apnea, and medication side effects [N4-R1][N4-R5]. These are less urgent than stroke, but still worth ruling out because they can affect speech and communication [N4-R1][N4-R5].

So, the most likely diagnosis is not a single fixed answer. The branch reports suggest that **aphasia, stroke, dysarthria, dementia, and other medical causes** are the main possibilities, depending on how the symptoms started and what else is happening [N1-R1][N1-R4][N5-R1][N2-F2][N3-R2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

---

## 2) Which symptoms suggest a serious or urgent problem?

The branch reports make this very clear: **sudden speech changes with sudden weakness, confusion, or facial drooping are red flags for stroke or acute brain injury** [N2-F2][N5-F3][N7-R5].

### **Red flags for urgent care**
- **Sudden slurred speech or confusion** [N2-F2][N5-F3]
- **Face weakness or drooping** [N2-F2][N5-F3]
- **Weakness in one arm or down one side of the body** [N2-F2][N5-F3]
- **Difficulty finding words** [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Sudden trouble reading or writing** [N1-R1][N1-F1]
